chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Safwan from Isma'il ibn Jabir said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'The time for prayer enters upon me while I am traveling, so I do not pray until I enter to my family.' He said: 'Pray and complete the prayer.' I said: 'The time for prayer enters upon me while I am with my family, intending to travel, so I do not pray until I leave.' He said: 'Then pray and shorten (the prayer), for if you do not do so, you have differed from the Messenger of Allah, by Allah, may Allah bless him and his family.'

Because the reason for combining these two rulings is that whoever returns from his journey and the time remains for the duration of completing (the prayer), it is upon him to pray in full. And if he fears missing the time, it is upon him to shorten. And likewise is the ruling for whoever departs for travel: if he fears missing the time, he shortens; and if there is time upon him, he completes. And that which indicates this is what he narrated:

key_terms.اَلتَّقْصِيرُ: Shortening the prayer (two rak'ahs) for travelers
key_terms.اَلتَّمَامِ: Completing the prayer (four rak'ahs) as if in one's hometown

ai.seo_question: When should a traveler shorten or complete their prayers during travel?
ai.summary: This hadith from Sahih al-Tusi clarifies the juristic distinction between returning travelers, who are generally required to pray fully (tamm) if they arrive with sufficient time, and departing travelers, who are encouraged to shorten (qasr) to avoid missing the prayer window. It highlights the practical principle of 'avoiding the loss of prayer' (khawf al-fawt), prioritizing the validity of the act over the length of the prayer when time is constrained. The narration underscores the flexibility within Shia fiqh to accommodate the physical realities of travel while maintaining strict adherence to prayer times.
